doc.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Chesky and RCA record deals
summary: How the Chesky record with Hinton and Terry led to RCA and a big-budget Christmas record.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Wow. You’ve had, it seems like, pretty good success with record label support. I was looking at your Christmas album and I’m seeing Don Sebesky, Pat Williams, Clare Fisher.

This will only take 25 minutes. Talk about blessed, I mean everywhere along the way, something good happened. And so Chesky Records makes a record of Johnny Frigo and me and Bucky, Ron Carter or Michael Moore and Butch Miles playing with Johnny © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

Frigo, you know, a violin player. And we all sat around the mic and play acoustic jazz, and then Chesky, David and Norman Chesky, the had just started the label. They go like, “We’re looking for a male singer, you know any male singers who could be on—” I said “Why don’t you come hear my group?” So they’d come to the thing, they’d hear my trio up at Jay’s when it used to be a great club here in New York, and I finished the set and David Chesky says, “well we’re going to get Milt Hinton and Clark Terry and your dad and we’ll make a record with you singing. And I’m like looking at them. Okay. And we get — McKenna’s in town so we get Dave McKenna, and just for good measure we get Connie Kay on the drums. It was either Connie Kay or Mel Lewis. And God bless them both. And Mel couldn’t make it so we got Connie Kay. And I’m sitting there looking at these guys, going okay, “My Blue Heaven” fellas? Yeah, sure [scats] and everybody’s going to the ball game and I’m sitting — oh my God. So I’m thinking I’d better play good you know. So that record gets me to RCA, because Harry Connick was becoming a star and RCA, Steve Backer was looking for a vocalist. He comes in to see me at The Algonquin and he says, “let’s get you on the label.” And they come out with a decent enough budget to make a big band record with, Dick Lieb did the arrangements. We made two records, made a bunch of records, and when you’re at RCA, or like Novus at the time which was a hot label, and then guys at RCA got mad that Novus was the hot label so like Steve Backer all of a sudden wasn’t around anymore and there was another new guy. Well we make our way, the presidents change and a new president, a guy from Canada, Bob Jameson comes in. He gets friendly with my manager, because I say Bob Jameson loves me, he’s seen me in Canada a bunch of times. Okay. Bob says let’s move him up to the big label. All right I’m up on the big leagues now, it’s like me and Dave Matthews on the label. And they get this guy, Ron Fair, and he says, he’s like one of their rock & roll guys, a young guy, but he’s like a retro guy, because that’s the big word everybody’s using in 1995, it’s very retro, and Pizzarelli’s very retro, what am I? Okay. We’ve got do a Christmas record with you and we’ll get all the best arrangers and this way, you know because they’ll play it every year, and it’s a good way to introduce you to people who wouldn’t listen to you because it’s Christmas songs, everybody buys Christmas records. And we’ll get — who do you want to get? We’ll get Johnny Mandel, we’ll get Ralph Burns. And I’m going is this guy serious? Okay. I went sure. They spent $250,000. I mean whatever anybody wanted, they got. They got Capitol Stude records, you know, Studios, where Nat Cole made all his records. And I’m going okay. And there’s Clare Fischer, and there’s John Clayton, there’s Patrick Williams, there’s Johnny Mandel, there’s Michel Legrand and his entire French orchestra who just came in off a plane to play a concert, and that was a whole story in itself.
